title: Alcohol is Bad Medicine in Bipolar Disorder
subtitle: Drinking alcohol to cope leads to a worse life
text:
I don't drink. I don't smoke. I use drugs. I never have. I also have bipolar disorder. These decisions about life are related. The fact that I enjoy, in theory, being correct is tempered by the grim reality for so many people who are not me. Alcohol is dumpster-fire lighting life choice for those with bipolar disorder. Welcome to The Frontier Psychiatrists.

A recent rather large study followed patients who both had bipolar disorder and reported how much they were drinking. Alcohol misuse is very common in bipolar disorder, with twice as many men > women impacted.

In clinical studies, AUDs affected more than one in three subjects with BD. Significant heterogeneity was found, which was largely explained by the geographical location of study populations and gender ratio of participants. AUDs affected more than one in five women and two in five men.1

These are people with Bipolar Disorder who have their act together enough to be in a clinical trial, and thus, not representative of people who are just, ya know, partying!

This is actually a more complex issue than my joke belies—those who develop bipolar disorder first—before they start drinking—actually have a more severe course of illness than those who started drinking in a alcohol use disordered way prior to the onset of their bipolar disorder.2

And prior sudies have found that despite this “alcohol-first” lower risk effect, those who keep drinking over the course of their bipolar disorder have a worse course of illness:

increased alcohol use preceded the development of new mood episodes. Four out of 5 studies examining the association between alcohol and rapid cycling indicated that AUDs were associated with higher rates of rapid-cycling.3

Keep in mind, when a research scientist is talking about “development of new mood episodes”—this is a sanitized version of what it is experienced for a patient and their family with these problems. A new episode is a month, or several, or a year, in which somebody is tortured. The demons are clawing at the door of one’s mind, relationships are being rent asunder, children are watching their sick parents as verbal (or even physical) domestic violence risk increases. There is little benign about the volatility of “new mood episodes” in bipolar disorder. Rapid cycling? That is defined as four or more episodes in a year. Nothing about this is trivial. The term self medication comes up a lot, among people living with bipolar disorder, as if alcohol can calm the demons that the medication's can’t or won’t.

I’ve got bad news. In fairness, science has bad news. I’m just the messenger. Alcohol is bad medicine…4

Drinking more led to more subsequent depression:

A person reporting alcohol use above their own mean amount [a.k.a. more than usual] tended to experience more depressive symptoms at the next time point, but increased depressive symptoms were not associated with greater subsequent alcohol use (β = 0.04; 95% CrI, 0.01-0.07)

And more subsequent mania:

Regarding mania or hypomania, alcohol use exceeding one’s own mean amount was associated with an increase in manic or hypomanic symptoms at the next time point, but not vice versa (β = 0.04; 95% CrI, 0.01-0.07])

To break this down, people who drank more got more depressed or more manic later. People who are more depressed? They did not subsequently drink more. The drinking more than usual preceded the increased symptoms. My interpretation of this is Alcohol is medicine that makes you sicker, not sickness leading to more consumption of alcohol—at least in this data set.

It is not just worse moods…it leads to worse performance at work:

A person reporting alcohol use above [the amount they usually drink] tended to experience a decrease in work functioning at the next time point (β = 0.03; 95% CrI, 0.00-0.06)

The sample was large but under-represented non-white individuals on a whole US population basis, limiting generalizability (but representative of the catchment area of this longitudinal sample).

This study included 584 participants (386 females (66.1%), 197 males (33.7%); mean [SD] age, 40 [13.6] years; 5 individuals self-reported as Asian [0.9%], 39 as Black or African American [6.7%], 21 as Hispanic or Latino [3.6%], 3 as Native American or Alaskan Native [0.5%], 511 as White [87.5%], and 15 as being of more than 1 race and ethnicity [2.6%], with 11 individuals not disclosing [1.9%]).

Bipolar disorder is a disabling condition. Alcohol makes it worse. People who have bipolar disorder should be advised not to drink alcohol, and all of us who drink less alcohol? We make the world a less risky place for people with bipolar disorder.

My wife and I started drinking Curious Elixirs (yes, that is an promo link…5) as non-alcoholic cocktails. And we're really into it. I'm really into it because I don't drink, ever, because I have bipolar disorder. I don't want my life to be horrible. My wife has gotten on the Mocktail train because they're good. It turns out that alcohol makes you feel kind of sh*tty, no matter what. But the more of us who don’t drink, and normalize non-alcoholic beverages, as part of our lives, makes the world a less normatively alcoholic place— and that is better for people with bipolar disorder. Think of it as a public health intervention for all of us, particularly the most vulnerable.
